newsitem.title: USA: U.S. tin market eyes trader personnel changes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tin market eyes trader personnel changes.

text.p: Personnel changes at two U.S. tin trading companies has prompted speculation about how the market may be divided in future, especially for the more expensive low lead metal.
Charles Rowan, group financial director of AMC, said Bernard Silverstein, currently vice president at Silex World Trade Inc, will be joining AMC's U.S. division, Amalgamet Inc, to trade tin.
Silverstein takes over "shortly" from Colin Wakeling, who left Amalgamet because of "differences over strategy", Rowan said.
"I think it doesn't indicate any great change in the way we do things. We will be continuing to do things we have done before," Rowan said.
But the changes have led to some speculation among the U.S. tin trade as to whether Silex will continue to trade tin after Silverstein leaves.

Several traders noted privately that Silverstein was the main tin trader at Silex, and the trading house's position in the market may change after he leaves. "My guess is that eventually Silex will exit the market, which is good because it's getting smaller and smaller," a producer official said.
"Silex will remain in the business and they are committed to tin and to whatever contracts they have on the books, on the sales side and on the supply side," Silverstein said.

Silex, along with Toyota Tsusho America, Inc and Metallgesellschaft's subsidiary, Henry Bath, are the three trading houses that sell low lead tin produced by Bolivia's Empresa Metalurgica Vinto in the U.S. market.

Traders said Vinto has just concluded deals with all three for next year for tonnages similar to those sold in 1996 - 400 tonnes per month for Toyota, and 300 tonnes per month each for Silex and Henry Bath.
Silverstein declined to discuss next year's Vinto deal with Silex.
Amalgamet also sells Vinto's material, but it is obtained through its arrangement with the Bolivian smelter to toll tin concentrates produced by Peru's Minsur.
Silverstein, like Wakeling, will be Amalgamet's sole tin trader in the U.S., but the office, which was based in Houston, will be moved to New Jersey, Silverstein said.
Meanwhile business in the U.S. remains fairly quiet with some reports of demand picking up.

Grade A metal premiums over LME cash are quoted at $160 to $180 per tonne or 7 to 8 cents per pound, with premiums on 50 parts per million low lead material at $200 to $240 per tonne or 9 to 10.8 cents.
Silverstein said the market was starting to pick up a little bit with more low lead material going to Europe.
"And the glut of low lead over here, we are not going to see a repeat of that next year," Silverstein said. "There is a lot of pent up business to be done."
